package_info.package_manager: N/A (Linux malware, not distributed via package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: OrBit is a Linux malware that implements advanced evasion techniques, gains persistence by hooking key system functions, provides remote access over SSH, harvests credentials, and logs TTY commands. Its behavior is explicitly designed for unauthorized access, credential theft, and covert persistence, which are all hallmarks of malicious software.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (on system boot or user login)
execution_context.file_location: shared object library injected into system processes (e.g., /lib/liborbit.so or via LD_PRELOAD)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the malware uses LD_PRELOAD to inject a malicious shared object into system processes, hooking key libc functions to intercept credentials and commands, enabling credential harvesting and command logging.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Using LD_PRELOAD to inject a shared object into system processes is a common technique for rootkits and malware to intercept sensitive data and evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely uses LD_PRELOAD for system-wide credential interception or command logging; such behavior is typical of malware.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: LD_PRELOAD is sometimes used by developers for debugging or performance monitoring, but not for credential harvesting.
key_indicators: LD_PRELOAD set globally or for system services
Shared object hooks authentication or TTY functions

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when user authenticates or executes commands)
execution_context.file_location: malicious shared object (liborbit.so) loaded into memory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Hooked functions: read(), write(), open(), execve(), pam_authenticate()
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the malware hooks authentication and I/O functions to intercept credentials and log TTY commands, exfiltrating sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hooking authentication and I/O functions is a classic rootkit technique for credential theft and activity monitoring.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal shared objects do not intercept authentication or TTY data for exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Security auditing tools may hook similar functions, but with user consent and transparency.
key_indicators: Interception of TTY and credential data

execution_context.file_location: malicious shared object (liborbit.so) persists on disk and in memory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Backdoor SSH access via hardcoded credentials or hidden user
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the malware provides remote access to the attacker over SSH, bypassing normal authentication controls, enabling persistent unauthorized access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Backdoor SSH access is a direct violation of system security and is a hallmark of persistent malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not create hidden SSH backdoors or bypass authentication.
key_indicators: Hidden SSH user or hardcoded credentials

attack_chain.action: Malware is deployed and persists by injecting a malicious shared object via LD_PRELOAD.
Malware hooks authentication and I/O functions to intercept credentials and log TTY commands.
Malware provides remote SSH access to attacker, bypassing normal authentication.

behavioral_signatures: LD_PRELOAD set for system processes or globally
Hooking of authentication and I/O functions (e.g., pam_authenticate, execve)
Unexpected logging of TTY commands or credential data
Unauthorized SSH access or hidden users
file_indicators: Persistence mechanisms referencing malicious shared objects
network_indicators: Outbound SSH connections from unexpected users
Exfiltration of credential or TTY data to external IPs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for suspicious use of LD_PRELOAD and modifications to /etc/ld.so.preload, scan for unauthorized shared objects in system library paths, detect hooks on authentication and I/O functions, audit for unexpected SSH access or hidden users, and monitor for exfiltration of sensitive data over the network.
